title: The Highest Compliment a Leader Can Receive
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The essay is structured as a deliberate ascent through three kinds of praise. The first is praise for results, which leaders are entitled to enjoy when a record of good outcomes accumulates. The second, higher, is the satisfaction of seeing people one has coached go on to do great things, especially when a protege outgrows the leader in career or accolades. The third and highest is not about outcomes at all: the observation, offered by someone who has watched you work, that you clearly love to lead. The piece is explicit about why this ranks first, because it speaks to the act of leadership rather than to what the leadership produced, and it supplies the parallel forms the compliment takes in other roles, parent and spouse among them. Its practical turn is a small one and easy to miss: given how hard leading is, people rarely say out loud how much they relish the privilege of it, and the essay asks the reader to make that passion visible in both expression and enthusiasm.
points: The three-rung structure is the argument: praise for results, then for those you developed, then for the evident love of the work itself.
The top rung is distinguished on a clear principle, that it speaks to the act of leading rather than to the outcomes leading produced, which is why it cannot be manufactured.
The protege rung contains a demanding test, taking deeper satisfaction when someone you coached surpasses your own career or accolades.
The compliment is shown in its parallel forms for parent and spouse, which generalises the point beyond work without diluting it.
The practical ask is small and specific: say out loud that you love to lead, because the difficulty of the work makes people forget to express the passion behind it.
quotes: Leaders who understand their distinct role in developing others find even deeper satisfaction when those they have nurtured and coached go on to do great things.
This is especially true when protégés go on to an even more successful career or more noteworthy accolades than the leader.
Perhaps nothing represents the badge of great leadership than to be proud of those who follow for the extraordinary achievements they have created.
More than results, track record, or team members’ achievements, this compliment stands out for what it says about the act of leadership, not for the outcomes leaders produce.
Ask the most admired leaders for the highest compliment they can receive and many will tell you it is an observation offered by those who witness their leadership work.
Leadership is hard. Too often we forget to share how much passion we have for the privilege of leading others.
